Departures & Arrivals

A move in Emigration is not a number changing in a ledger. The people who leave take a worked tile with them, spend turns on the road, and have to be given somewhere to live when they arrive. This page follows one population point from the settlement it leaves to the one it joins.
Leaving

When a population point leaves a settlement, the mod removes one of its outlying rural improvements along with the yields it produced, so the land empties as the people go. Pillaged tiles are abandoned first. In a starving city, food tiles are kept as long as possible. Otherwise plain tiles go before resource tiles and distant plots before near ones, and a Cultural Enclave's tile is never chosen. The emptied rural district is cleared shortly afterwards so the city can grow onto the tile again later.

A settlement can only lose so many people in one turn (two by default, on the Medium intensity preset), and each crisis is capped as a whole: a single siege displaces at most 60% of the population the city had when it began, and a single disaster at most 50%. The deaths a long crisis causes (see When There Is No Refuge) sit outside these caps.
On the Road

Migrants are not teleported. They leave the moment they depart and arrive after a delay that grows with the distance to their destination, up to a cap (four turns by default; slower game speeds stretch it). War refugees always spend at least a turn on the road. If their destination is captured or razed while they travel, or stays too full to receive them, they perish in transit and are counted among the losses, not the arrivals.

A destination can only take in so many newcomers per turn (four by default). Arrivals beyond that cap wait and try again the next turn, the longest-waiting first, so a boomtown cannot swallow dozens at once.
Arriving

Other civilizations place their own arrivals. For your cities, the setting How newcomers settle (Options, Add-ons, Emigration, Advanced settings, Arrivals & departures) decides what happens when a point arrives:[BLIST][LI][B]Ask me[/B] (the default): a pop-up titled Newcomers in, or Refugees in, the receiving city lets you choose the tile, let the city decide, or wait. Three switches beside it choose which kinds of arrival ask; out of the box only refugees do, while migrants and returning people are placed at once.[LI][B]Automatic[/B]: the city places the point immediately, as it does when it grows.[LI][B]Migrant unit[/B]: the newcomers arrive as a Migrant unit beside the city, for you to resettle where you like. An unsettled Migrant costs its owner upkeep every turn, so they are not meant to be hoarded.[LI][B]Off[/B]: the game's own Grow City prompt asks you to place the point, exactly as for natural growth.[/LIST]

The Refugees pop-up names where the arrivals fled from and what they fled, and carries a quotation in the voice of that people (see Voices of the Displaced). Refugees from a civilization you have not met are described only as displaced, so the pop-up never reveals them.
Refugees Waiting to Settle

War and disaster refugees do not all find a home the day they arrive. Most enter a waiting pool at their destination and settle over the following turns; a share (one in five by default) settles at once. A happy, open, uncrowded host settles them faster, an Anti-Immigration Stance slows them, and the host pays upkeep for those still waiting. If the crisis they fled reaches their new city, those still waiting are the first to move on. The city readout and the City Details panel show how many are waiting.
The Cost of Taking People In

Each newcomer adds an integration load to the receiving civilization. While it lasts (it fades over roughly six to eight turns), the civilization pays [icon:YIELD_GOLD] Gold each turn and its accumulated [icon:YIELD_HAPPINESS] Happiness is drawn down, which delays its next Celebration; no settlement is made locally unhappy by it. A civilization busy settling many arrivals also becomes a less attractive destination for still more, a congestion brake that wealth alone does not remove. See Integration & the Cost of Growth; any of these costs can be set to 0 in Advanced settings.
Calling Your People Home

When war, disaster or famine has driven your people out of a settlement, you need not wait for return migration to bring them back on its own. Once no settlement of yours is under war, siege, disaster or famine and some of your people still live away from the settlement they fled, the mod offers a call to bring them home. It arrives as a dialog and comes in two forms, depending on where your people are now; a homecoming quotation in your own people's voice heads it (see Voices of the Displaced). You can also decline and leave them where they are: they may still drift home on their own in time.
From Your Own Settlements

People who fled to another of your settlements are inside your borders and under your rule, so a call for them is a purchase: choose how many to bring home, pay, and exactly that many return, from the largest group first. The dialog names the settlement they are pulled back from and the one they return to.
From Foreign Cities

People who fled to a city of another civilization have a life there, and a foreign ruler has no reason to help you empty their streets. A call for them is a gamble: the dialog names the city and its ruler and states the odds for each person (about 18% by default). Every person asked is rolled, the call is paid for at the size you chose whether or not anyone answers, and it may bring nobody. An unanswered call is written into the Chronicle and still starts the cooldown, so it cannot simply be repeated next turn.
Prices and Cooldowns

Each call offers a ladder of sizes (one person, about half of what is callable, and everyone) in [icon:YIELD_GOLD] Gold or in [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence, and only the sizes your treasury can cover. Prices climb faster than the head count (two people cost nearly three times one, three about five times), calls abroad cost more still, and every age past Antiquity multiplies the price (three times in the Exploration Age, nine times in the Modern Age), so a call keeps its weight as treasuries grow. After a call, the same civilization must wait eight turns before calling again.

Tip: a community that has taken root as a Cultural Enclave is far less inclined to go home on its own, so a call is the surest way to bring such people back. The whole feature, the offer, the prices and the odds are under Calling people home in Advanced settings.
Immigration Policies

Emigration adds policy cards to the civics of every age. They appear in the policy chooser like any other card, can be slotted and swapped freely, and stack with the diplomatic Open Borders agreement, which increases migration both ways between the two signatories. Their migration effects are the mod's own; the flat yields on each card are native game effects. Borders & Influence, Attraction & Asylum and Talent Raids describe how they play; this page lists them.
Antiquity Age

[BLIST][LI][B]Pro-Immigration Stance[/B] (Citizenship): immigration to your cities rises by 50%; +1 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn.[LI][B]Anti-Immigration Stance[/B] (Citizenship): immigration falls by 60% and 40% fewer of your own citizens leave for rival civilizations; refugees you still take in settle more slowly; +2 [icon:YIELD_PRODUCTION] Production in every city, -2 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn.[/LIST]
Exploration Age

[BLIST][LI][B]Pro-Immigration Stance[/B] (Economics): immigration rises by 50%; +2 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn.[LI][B]Anti-Immigration Stance[/B] (Economics): immigration falls by 60%, 40% fewer citizens leave for rivals, refugees settle more slowly; +3 [icon:YIELD_PRODUCTION] Production in every city, -3 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn.[LI][B]Talent Attraction[/B] (Inspiration): +1 [icon:YIELD_SCIENCE] Science each turn, plus about +1.5 more for every immigrant you attract, up to +12; the bonus fades if immigration stops.[LI][B]Cultural Magnetism[/B] (Society): the same, in [icon:YIELD_CULTURE] Culture.[LI][B]Commercial Draw[/B] (Mercantilism): the same, in [icon:YIELD_GOLD] Gold.[LI][B]Selective Asylum[/B] (Piety): refugees fleeing war and disaster are strongly drawn to you, the most desperate first; +1 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn.[/LIST]
Modern Age

[BLIST][LI][B]Pro-Immigration Stance[/B] (Social Question): immigration rises by 50%; +3 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn.[LI][B]Anti-Immigration Stance[/B] (Social Question): immigration falls by 60%, 40% fewer citizens leave for rivals, refugees settle more slowly; +4 [icon:YIELD_PRODUCTION] Production in every city, -4 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn.[LI][B]Talent Attraction[/B] (Modernization): +2 [icon:YIELD_SCIENCE] Science each turn, plus about +1.5 more per immigrant, up to +12, fading when immigration stops.[LI][B]Cultural Magnetism[/B] (Natural History): the same, in [icon:YIELD_CULTURE] Culture.[LI][B]Commercial Draw[/B] (Capitalism): the same, in [icon:YIELD_GOLD] Gold.[LI][B]Refugee Compact[/B] (Political Theory): refugees fleeing war and disaster are strongly drawn to you, the most desperate first; +2 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence and +1 [icon:YIELD_CULTURE] Culture each turn.[/LIST]
Tip: the attraction cards pay for themselves only while people keep arriving. Pair one with a Pro-Immigration Stance, Open Borders or an asylum card, and switch it out when the inflow dries up.
Map Lenses

Emigration adds two lenses to the map, both listed in the game's lens panel and each with a hotkey. Both follow the mod's visibility setting (see Scope & Visibility), and while one is up the game's own tile tooltip is hidden so the lens's readout is never covered.
Prosperity Lens (Shift+P)

The Prosperity lens paints every settled tile by what stands on it, so you can see at a glance where a settlement's prosperity really lives. A tile's prosperity is a sum of named points: a wonder on the hex (+6, the largest term), the city centre (+3), each building (+2, plus +1 for a completed quarter), a worked improvement (+1), the hex's own yield (+1 per 3), a river (+1), a natural wonder on the hex (+3) or next door (+2 each), a wonder next door (+1 each), and anything pillaged on the hex (-3 each) or next door (-1 each). The scale is absolute, so a wonder tile reads the same in every settlement, and banded: Flourishing (8 or more), Thriving (5 to 7), Ordinary (2 to 4), Meagre (0 to 1) and Blighted (below 0), on a grey-to-green and grey-to-red gradient. Water a settlement has not built on is not painted.

Hover a tile and the cursor panel lists its band, its score and every term behind it, then the settlement's standing in the migration model: its Prosperity score, whether it is gaining or losing people, and why. Wonders and natural wonders are recognised from the game's own database, so ones added by an age or another mod count too.
Ethnic Composition Lens (Shift+E)

Every settlement keeps a ledger of where its people came from, by the civilization each person descends from, and the Ethnic Composition lens draws that ledger on the map as a per-tile mosaic. The dense urban core takes the dominant origin's colour; each smaller community is seated on a share-proportional number of tiles, denser tiles first, its colour thinned by how few they are. A community that has a standing Cultural Enclave is seated on the enclave's tile first, so that tile reads as their quarter; where no enclave stands, no tile may read past the share an enclave requires, so a community still short of one shows as a lighter tint. Hover a settled tile for its exact mix.
Enclave Markers

A Cultural Enclave has no art of its own; its tile borrows a real improvement's model. So every enclave tile carries a marker with the origin civilization's symbol, and hovering it shows the mod's own tooltip instead of the borrowed improvement's: the enclave's name and stage (established, recognized, contested or fading), the yields the tile works and why, what the enclave's people built there, what the improvement it replaced still pays the city, and the stance yields the city gains and loses each turn.
Notifications & the City Readout
Toasts

Migration announces itself with toasts in the game's own typography. They stack, stay about eleven seconds, and are coloured by cause: green is kept for people gained in your own cities, while departures and losses use neutral, amber or crisis colours. Counts are given in population points and in people, for example 3 population points (36,000 people); the Population unit of measurement option chooses one or both. Disasters are named with the game's own event names, wars by their name, and a conquest by the city taken.

The default is deliberately selective: only the largest event of a pass toasts, and cooldowns and thresholds keep a busy world quiet. The Notifications section of Advanced settings offers a verbose mode with a toast per cause, or none at all; every notification that fires is written to the log either way.
The Notifications Log

The Notifications tab of the Migration dashboard keeps a permanent, scrollable log of every notification, newest first, up to the last 120: the turn, the cause and the named event, the settlement people left, where they went, and how many. Each entry expands to its detail. The Migration Chronicle's history entries, an exodus, a diaspora taking root, a homecoming, an enclave recognized or faded, the outcome of every refugee decision and every call home, appear in the same list.
The City Readout

When you select one of your cities, a small panel explains its migration at a glance: the pressures on it (unhappiness, war, disaster, famine, overcrowding), whether it is gaining or losing people and how fast, the likely destination of anyone who leaves, what its newcomers are costing, refugees still waiting to settle, progress toward a Cultural Enclave, and a line of advice. A warning marks a city whose people are trapped with nowhere to flee.
City Details

The game's own City Details panel gains two Emigration sections. Under Citizen Growth: the city's people by origin, its emigration with destinations, its immigration with origins, and refugees held awaiting settlement. Under Building Breakdown: the city's Cultural Enclave, if it has one. Both read the live game when the panel opens and update as you switch cities.
Options & Intensity

All of Emigration's settings live under Options, Add-ons, in the main menu and in game. The Add-ons tab holds the everyday settings; an Advanced settings button opens the rest. Settings apply at once, or at the start of the next migration pass.
Intensity Presets

The Intensity preset sets, in one choice, how often people move and how hard wars uproot them: the per-turn limits, how far people will travel, and how strongly violence pushes them out.[BLIST][LI][B]Low[/B]: people move rarely and in small numbers; a city loses at most one point and gains at most two per turn; sieges displace slowly.[LI][B]Medium[/B] (the default): the shipped balance; at most two out and four in per city per turn.[LI][B]High[/B]: frequent, large movements; up to four out and eight in per city per turn, faster flight and heavier war surges.[/LIST]Changing one of the settings a preset controls in Advanced settings shows the preset as Custom.
Everyday Settings

[BLIST][LI][B]Population unit of measurement[/B]: show moves as Civilization population points, as historically scaled people (matching the Demographics mod), or both.[LI][B]Movement between civilizations[/B], and three [B]Refugees from conflict[/B] sliders (overall, from wars between major powers, from raids by minor powers), scale those flows without touching anything else.[LI][B]Dashboard data[/B]: live migration, or sample data to preview the network before real flows build up; [B]Migration timeline detail[/B], how often the network records a snapshot for its timeline; [B]Simplify dashboard[/B], which hides the heavy Network and Causes views; and the [B]Dashboard dock button[/B].[LI]On/off switches for [B]notifications[/B], [B]ethnic integration[/B], [B]return migration[/B] and [B]refugee decisions[/B].[LI][B]Analytics visibility[/B]: whether the dashboard and lenses show civilizations you have not met (see Scope & Visibility).[/LIST]
Advanced Settings

The Advanced settings window lists every one of the mod's individual settings, more than a hundred, in collapsible sections: Pacing, Scope, Border policies, Prosperity model, War & violence, Disasters, Geography & movement, Integration costs, Balance brakes, Arrivals & departures, Cultural enclaves, Calling people home, Attrition, Notifications, Readouts & rankings and Visuals. Sections start collapsed and the ones you open stay open. Values show their units (55%, x1.5, 3 turns) or a word (Off, Instant); the window has a search box, a marker on every changed setting, a reset for each and Reset all. Per-leader and per-civilization tuning (see Leaders & Civilizations) has its own switch here.
Game Speed

Every turn-based pace in the mod scales with game speed, from Online to Marathon: cooldowns, time in transit, integration periods, the enclave dwell and fade clocks, decision cooldowns and the rest, so a Marathon game sees the same migrations spread over proportionally more turns. Population counts are not scaled.
The Demographics Mod

Emigration works on its own, but with the Demographics mod installed it also registers an Emigration tab in the Demographics screen and shares its people-scaling with it, so a population point means the same number of people in both. The Migration dashboard's tabs appear there as sub-tabs, and the Migration page in Demographics opens the dashboard. Nothing changes if Demographics is absent or too old; the registration is silently skipped.
Graphs and Tables

[BLIST][LI][B]Net Migration (Graph)[/B]: cumulative arrivals minus departures, by civilization.[LI][B]Net Migration (Table)[/B]: the same value with a diverging bar, beside the movement behind it in three groups, Internal (moves between a civilization's own settlements), External (moves across a border, which is what Net measures) and Total, each counting people who left and people who arrived.[LI][B]Emigration[/B] and [B]Immigration[/B]: gross outflow and inflow, with cause breakdowns.[LI][B]Refugees (Left / Arrived)[/B]: displaced people sent and received, with optional war and disaster markers on the timeline.[/LIST]A Data section toggles the metrics and the unit, scaled people or raw population points, and Demographics' war-effects tooltip can show a Refugees row drawn from Emigration's numbers.
Voices of the Displaced

Whenever the mod puts displaced people in front of you, it lets them speak for themselves. Each pop-up that concerns refugees, migrants, a returning diaspora or a settled foreign community carries a short quotation in the voice of that people: an actual refugee, exile or migrant of theirs where such words survive, and a witness who wrote of them with dignity where they do not. The pages that follow list every quotation the mod can show, the situation it appears in, and who the speaker was.
Where the Voices Appear

[BLIST][LI][B]The refugee decision[/B] (Refugees at the Border, The Sick at the Gates): a refugee's words from the people fleeing.[LI][B]The Refugees pop-up[/B] that asks where refugees reaching one of your cities should live: the same refugee voices.[LI][B]The Newcomers pop-up[/B] for migrants who chose to come: a migrant's words from their people.[LI][B]The call-home dialog[/B]: the words of someone of your own civilization who longed for home, or came back to it.[LI][B]The Cultural Enclave decision[/B]: a line from the enclave people's own writers, inscriptions or proverbs; the first enclave of a people in your empire shows one line, the second another.[/LIST]The line is fixed by the event, so reloading a save shows the same words. When a people has no voice of its own for a situation, or comes from a civilization you have not met, the pop-up draws on the general pools of Voices of Many Lands, which never name a people.
How the Quotations Were Chosen

Every line was located in a readable copy of its source before it shipped. Quotation websites did not count, and a modern historian's paraphrase in quotation marks is not a quote. Cuts are marked with an ellipsis, and no line is extended past where its source ends. A published translation names its translator; (trans.) without a name is the mod's own rendering of the verified original. Enclave lines prefer a people's own writers, inscriptions and proverbs. Refugee and migrant lines prefer an actual refugee, exile or migrant of that people, then a witness who wrote of them with dignity; otherwise the people has no line of its own and the pools speak.

No quotation may generalize a people's character or pair them with a stereotype, frame the displaced as invaders, a burden or a threat, quote a perpetrator of atrocities or a hate figure, trivialize sacred text, or dwell on graphic trauma. Where a source passes these tests only in part, the excerpt shown is the part that does. The full record of every quotation's source, and of the lines that were checked and rejected, is published with the mod's documentation.
Original Languages

Where the original is not English, the mod keeps it beside an English rendering. The game's fonts cannot draw Arabic, Hebrew, Greek, Cyrillic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Georgian, Mongolian, the Indic and Southeast Asian scripts, or the Chinese, Japanese and Korean scripts, so for those you see the English alone. Latin-script originals, from Old English and Old Norse to Vietnamese, Turkish and the transliterated Akkadian of the Assyrian inscriptions, are shown in full.
About Emigration

Emigration is a user-interface mod: each turn it reads the state of the world and writes population, tiles, yields and Influence back through the game's own commands. It changes no rule of the base game, replaces none of its files, adds only its own database rows, and never alters what the AI decides. It simulates every living major civilization from the first turn, whether or not you have met them. Its systems are described on the pages of this section, and the Guide tab of the Migration dashboard keeps a one-screen reference of what does and does not drive migration.

Version 3.0.0, for Civilization VII 1.5.0. The interface is available in twelve languages. The source, the full documentation with every formula, and the record of every quotation's source are published on GitHub at github.com/tmtmiller1/civilizationvii-emigration.
The People Behind the Numbers

Migration and displacement are abstracted here as game systems. In reality people most often leave home because of war, persecution, disaster or hardship, and this mod tries to acknowledge that without trivializing it: refugees are never framed as a threat or a burden, the displaced speak in their own words wherever their words survive, and a stricken city's losses are counted as deaths rather than as a statistic that vanishes. The author has marked the mod's milestones with donations to refugee relief. If you are able, consider supporting UNHCR, the International Rescue Committee, Médecins Sans Frontières, the International Refugee Assistance Project, or local refugee and mutual-aid groups.
Credits

Emigration is by Tower. Its Prosperity model adapts the Emigration mod for Civilization V by Tomahawk, Mk Z and Tim_The_Texan. Population scaling is aligned with the Demographics mod, and the Talent Raid diplomacy actions are provided by the Diplomacy Extended mod. Quotations are drawn from the published sources listed in the mod's documentation; translations marked (trans.) without a translator's name are the mod's own.
